Null-controllability of two species reaction-diffusion system with nonlinear coupling: a new duality method

Kévin Le Balc’h
Abstract.

We consider a 2×22\times 2 nonlinear reaction-diffusion system posed on a smooth bounded domain Ω\Omega of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} (N≥1N\geq 1). The control input is in the source term of only one equation. It is localized in some arbitrary nonempty open subset ω\omega of the domain Ω\Omega. First, we prove a global null-controllability result when the coupling term in the second equation is an odd power. As the linearized system around zero is not null-controllable, the usual strategy consists in using the return method, introduced by Jean-Michel Coron, or the method of power series expansions. In this paper, we give a direct nonlinear proof, which relies on a new duality method that we call Reflexive Uniqueness Method. It is a variation in reflexive Banach spaces of the well-known Hilbert Uniqueness Method, introduced by Jacques-Louis Lions. It is based on Carleman estimates in LpL^{p} (2≤p<∞2\leq p<\infty) obtained from the usual Carleman inequality in L2L^{2} and parabolic regularity arguments. This strategy enables us to find a control of the heat equation, which is an odd power of a regular function. Another advantage of the method is to produce small controls for small initial data. Secondly, thanks to the return method, we also prove a null-controllability result for more general nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems, where the coupling term in the second equation behaves as an odd power at zero.

1. Introduction

Let T>0T>0, N∈ℕ∗N\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, Ω\Omega be a bounded, connected, open subset of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} of class C2C^{2}, and let ω\omega be a nonempty open subset of Ω\Omega.
We consider a 2×22\times 2 nonlinear reaction-diffusion system with one internal control:

(NL) {∂tu−Δ​u=f1​(u,v)+h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−Δ​v=f2​(u,v)in⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=f_{1}(u,v)+h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta v=f_{2}(u,v)&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega,\end{array}\right.

with f1,f2∈C∞​(ℝ2,ℝ)f_{1},f_{2}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}) satisfying f1​(0,0)=f2​(0,0)=0f_{1}(0,0)=f_{2}(0,0)=0. Here, (u,v)(t,.):Ω→ℝ2(u,v)(t,.):\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} is the state to be controlled, h=h(t,.):Ω→ℝh=h(t,.):\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the control input supported in ω\omega.
We are interested in the null-controllability of (NL): for any initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}), does there exist a control hh such that the solution (u,v)(u,v) of (NL) verifies (u,v)(T,.)=(0,0)(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0)?

1.1. Context

The problem of null-controllability of the heat equation was solved independently by Gilles Lebeau, Luc Robbiano in 19951995 (see [25] or the survey [24]) and Andrei Fursikov, Oleg Imanuvilov in 19961996 (see [20]) with Carleman estimates.

Theorem 1.1.

[3, Corollary 2]
For every u0∈L2​(Ω)u_{0}\in L^{2}(\Omega), there exists h∈L2​((0,T)×Ω)h\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega) such that the solution uu of

{∂tu−Δ​u=h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,u=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,u(0,.)=u0in​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ u(0,.)=u_{0}&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega,\end{array}\right.

satisfies u(T,.)=0u(T,.)=0.

Then, null-controllability of linear and nonlinear coupled parabolic systems has been a challenging issue. For example, in [2], Farid Ammar-Khodja, Assia Benabdallah, Cédric Dupaix and Manuel Gonzalez-Burgos identified sharp conditions for the control of systems of the form

(1) {∂tU−D​Δ​U=A​U+B​H​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,U=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,U(0,.)=U0in​Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}U-D\Delta U=AU+BH1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ U=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ U(0,.)=U_{0}&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega.\end{array}\right.

where U(t,.):Ω→ℝnU(t,.):\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} is the state, H=H(t,.):Ω→ℝmH=H(t,.):\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} is the control, D:=d​i​a​g​(d1,…,dn)D:=diag(d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) with di∈(0,+∞)d_{i}\in(0,+\infty) is the diffusion matrix, A∈ℳn​(ℝ)A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{R}) (matrix with nn lines and nn columns with entries in ℝ\mathbb{R}) is the coupling matrix and B∈ℳn,m​(ℝ)B\in\mathcal{M}_{n,m}(\mathbb{R}) (matrix with nn lines and mm columns with entries in ℝ\mathbb{R}) represents the distribution of controls. In general, the rank of BB is less than nn (roughly speaking, there are less controls than equations), so that the controllability of the full system depends strongly on the (linear) coupling present in the system. We can see the survey [3] for other results (and open problems) on the controllability of linear coupled parabolic problems. The introduction of the article [23] provides an overview of the results on the controllability of linear and nonlinear coupled parabolic problems.
Roughly speaking, the null-controllability of (NL) can be reformulated as follows: how can the component vv be controlled thanks to the nonlinear coupling f2​(u,v)f_{2}(u,v)?

1.2. Linearization

We introduce the following notation which will be used throughout the paper,

∀τ>0,Qτ=(0,τ)×Ω.\forall\tau>0,\ Q_{\tau}=(0,\tau)\times\Omega.

The usual strategy consists in proving a local null-controllability result for (NL) from a (global) null-controllability result for the linearized system of (NL) around ((u¯,v¯),h¯)=((0,0),0)((\overline{u},\overline{v}),\overline{h})=((0,0),0). The linearized system (L) is

(L) {∂tu−Δ​u=∂f1∂u​(0,0)​u+∂f1∂v​(0,0)​v+h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−Δ​v=∂f2∂u​(0,0)​u+∂f2∂v​(0,0)​vin⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial u}(0,0)u+\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial v}(0,0)v+h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta v=\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(0,0)u+\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial v}(0,0)v&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega.\end{array}\right.
Definition 1.2.

System (L) is said to be null-controllable if
for every (u0,v0)∈L2​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}, there exists h∈L2​(QT)h\in L^{2}(Q_{T}) such that the solution (u,v)(u,v) of (L) satisfies (u,v)(T,.)=(0,0)(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).

Proposition 1.3.

[3, Theorem 7.1]
The following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    System (L) is null-controllable.

  2. (2)

    ∂f2∂u​(0,0)≠0\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(0,0)\neq 0.

Indeed, if ∂f2∂u​(0,0)=0\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(0,0)=0, then the equation on vv is decoupled from the first equation of (L). Consequently, for any initial data (u0,v0)∈L2​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{2}(\Omega)^{2} such that v0≠0v_{0}\neq 0, we have v(T,.)≠0v(T,.)\neq 0 by the backward uniqueness of the heat equation (see [5]). The proof of (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1) is a byproduct of Proposition 1.7.
Roughly speaking, uu can be driven to 00 thanks to the control hh and vv can be driven to 00 thanks to the coupling term ∂f2∂u​(0,0)​u\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(0,0)u. We have the following diagram

h​↝c​o​n​t​r​o​l​s​u​↝c​o​n​t​r​o​l​s​v.h\overset{controls}{\rightsquigarrow}u\overset{controls}{\rightsquigarrow}v.
Definition 1.4.

[Null-controllability]

  1. (1)

    System (NL) is said to be locally null-controllable if there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that for every (u0,v0)∈L∞​(Ω)2{(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2}} satisfying ‖(u0,v0)‖L∞​(Ω)2≤δ\left\lVert(u_{0},v_{0})\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2}}\leq\delta, there exists h∈L2​(QT)h\in L^{2}(Q_{T}) such that (NL) has a (unique) solution (u,v)∈L∞​(QT)2(u,v)\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})^{2} that satisfies (u,v)(T,.)=(0,0)(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).

    for every (u0,v0)∈L∞​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2}, there exists h∈L2​(QT)h\in L^{2}(Q_{T}) such that (NL) has a (unique) solution (u,v)∈L∞​(QT)2(u,v)\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})^{2} that satisfies (u,v)(T,.)=(0,0)(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).

Now, we mention the linear test for (NL) which is a corollary of Proposition 1.3.

Proposition 1.5.

[11, Proof of Theorem 1]
Let us suppose that ∂f2∂u​(0,0)≠0\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(0,0)\neq 0. Then, (NL) is locally null-controllable.

Remark 1.6.

This result is well-known but it is difficult to find in the literature (see [1, Theorem 6] with a restriction on the dimension 1≤N<61\leq N<6 and other function spaces or one can adapt the arguments given in [11] to get Proposition 1.5 for any N∈ℕ∗N\in\mathbb{N}^{*}). For other results in this direction, see [29], [26], [21] and [7].

The natural question is: what can we say about (NL) if the linearized system around ((0,0),0)((0,0),0) is not null-controllable i.e. when ∂f2∂u​(0,0)=0\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(0,0)=0?
Another strategy to get local null-controllability for (NL) consists in linearizing around a non trivial trajectory (u¯,v¯,h¯)∈C∞​(QT¯)3(\overline{u},\overline{v},\overline{h})\in C^{\infty}(\overline{Q_{T}})^{3} of the nonlinear system (NL) which goes from 00 to 00. This procedure is called the return method and was introduced by Jean-Michel Coron in [8] (see [9, Chapter 6]). The linearized system is the following one:

(L-bis) {∂tu−Δ​u=∂f1∂u​(u¯,v¯)​u+∂f1∂v​(u¯,v¯)​v+h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−Δ​v=∂f2∂u​(u¯,v¯)​u+∂f2∂v​(u¯,v¯)​vin⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial u}(\overline{u},\overline{v})u+\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial v}(\overline{u},\overline{v})v+h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta v=\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(\overline{u},\overline{v})u+\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial v}(\overline{u},\overline{v})v&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega.\end{array}\right.

First, let us recall the generalization of Proposition 1.3 when the coupling coefficients are not constant. Historically, the proof is due to Luz de Teresa in [13].

Proposition 1.7.

[3, Theorem 7.1]
We assume that there exist t1<t2∈(0,T)t_{1}<t_{2}\in(0,T), a nonempty open subset ω0⊂ω\omega_{0}\subset\omega and ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that |∂f2∂u​(u¯​(t,x),v¯​(t,x))|≥ε\left|\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(\overline{u}(t,x),\overline{v}(t,x))\right|\geq\varepsilon for every (t,x)∈(t1,t2)×ω0(t,x)\in(t_{1},t_{2})\times\omega_{0}. Then, system (L-bis) is null-controllable (in the sense of Definition 1.2).

Then, the linear test gives the following result.

Proposition 1.8.

[11, Proof of Theorem 1]
We assume that there exist t1<t2∈(0,T)t_{1}<t_{2}\in(0,T), a nonempty open subset ω0⊂ω\omega_{0}\subset\omega and ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that |∂f2∂u​(u¯,v¯)|≥ε\left|\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(\overline{u},\overline{v})\right|\geq\varepsilon on (t1,t2)×ω0(t_{1},t_{2})\times\omega_{0}. Then, system (NL) is locally null-controllable.

Proposition 1.8 is used used in [11] with f2​(u1,u2)=u13+R​u2f_{2}(u_{1},u_{2})=u_{1}^{3}+Ru_{2}, where R∈ℝR\in\mathbb{R}, [10], [12] and [23].

1.3. The “power system”

A model-system for the question of null-controllability when the linearized system around ((0,0),0)((0,0),0) is not null-controllable is the following one:

(Power) {∂tu−Δ​u=h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−Δ​v=unin⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta v=u^{n}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega,\end{array}\right.

where n≥2n\geq 2 is an integer.

Proposition 1.9.

If nn is an even integer, then (Power) is not locally null-controllable.

Indeed, by the maximum principle (un≥0u^{n}\geq 0), we have, for any solution of (Power) associated to an initial condition (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) with v0≥0v_{0}\geq 0 and v0≠0v_{0}\neq 0,

v(T,.)≥v~(T,.)≥0andv~(T,.)≠0,v(T,.)\geq\widetilde{v}(T,.)\geq 0\hskip 20.00003pt\text{and}\hskip 20.00003pt\widetilde{v}(T,.)\neq 0,

where v~\widetilde{v} is the solution of the heat equation

{∂tv~−Δ​v~=0in⁡(0,T)×Ω,v~=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,v~(0,.)=v0in​Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}\widetilde{v}-\Delta\widetilde{v}=0&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \widetilde{v}=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ \widetilde{v}(0,.)=v_{0}&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega.\end{array}\right.

The following result is due to Jean-Michel Coron, Sergio Guerrero and Lionel Rosier. The proof is based on the return method (see [11]).

Proposition 1.10.

[11, Theorem 1]
If n=3n=3, then (Power) is locally null-controllable.

Remark 1.11.

The difficult point of the proof of Proposition 1.10 is the construction of the nontrivial trajectory (see [11, Section 2]). The method can be generalized to n=2​k+1n=2k+1 for k∈ℕ∗k\in\mathbb{N}^{*} but with longer computations. The same problem appears in [31, Section 4.2].

Remark 1.12.

An homogeneity argument shows that for the system (Power) the local null-controllability implies the global null-controllability (consider uε=ε​uu_{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon u, vε=εn​vv_{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon^{n}v, hε=ε​hh_{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon h). However, this strategy does not provide estimate on the control. This kind of argument is used in [12]. In this paper, we propose a different direct method for the global null-controllability, that provides estimates.

1.4. A direct approach

From now on, k∈ℕ∗k\in\mathbb{N}^{*} is fixed.
The first goal of this paper is to give a direct proof (i.e. without return method) of the global null-controllability of the system

(Odd) {∂tu−Δ​u=h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−Δ​v=u2​k+1in⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta v=u^{2k+1}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega.\end{array}\right.

Our proof is based on a new duality method, called Reflexive Uniqueness Method. The first step will consist in proving a Carleman estimate in L2​k+2L^{2k+2} for the heat equation (see Section 4.1 and particularly Theorem 4.4). The second step will consist in considering a penalized problem in L2​k+22​k+1L^{\frac{2k+2}{2k+1}} (see Section 4.2), a generalization of the Penalized Hilbert Uniqueness Method, introduced by Jacques-Louis Lions (see [27] and also [32, Section 2] for an introduction to the Hilbert Uniqueness Method and some generalizations). This procedure enables us to find a control of the heat equation which is an odd power of a regular function.
The second goal of this paper is to prove a local null-controllability result for more general systems than (Odd) thanks to the return method (introduced in Section 1).

First, the well-posedness in WTlW_{T}^{l} (i.e. (4), (5) and (6)) is based on Galerkin approximations and energy estimates. One can easily adapt the arguments given in [16, Section 7.1.2].
Secondly, the LpL^{p}-estimate (i.e. (7) for p<+∞p<+\infty) is based on the application of (4) with a cut-off of w=|y|p−2​yw=|y|^{p-2}y.
Finally, the L∞L^{\infty}-estimate (i.e. (7) for p=+∞p=+\infty) is based on Stampacchia’s method (see the proof of [22, Chapter 3, Paragraph 7, Theorem 7.1]). ∎

The following definition-proposition justifies the notion of (unique) solution associated to a control and therefore, the definition of local null-controllability and global null-controllability (already introduced in Section 1, see Definition 1.4).

Definition-Proposition 2.4.

Let (u0,v0)∈L∞​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2}, h∈L2​(QT)h\in L^{2}(Q_{T}).

∀(w1,w2)∈L2​(0,T,H01​(Ω))2,\displaystyle\forall(w_{1},w_{2})\in L^{2}(0,T;H_{0}^{1}(\Omega))^{2},
(8) ∫0T(∂tu,w1)(H−1​(Ω),H01​(Ω))+∫QT∇u.∇w1=∫QT(f1​(u,v)+h​1ω)​w1,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}(\partial_{t}u,w_{1})_{(H^{-1}(\Omega),H_{0}^{1}(\Omega))}+\int_{Q_{T}}\nabla u.\nabla w_{1}=\int_{Q_{T}}(f_{1}(u,v)+h1_{\omega})w_{1},
(9) ∫0T(∂tv,w2)(H−1​(Ω),H01​(Ω))+∫QT∇v.∇w2=∫QTf2​(u,v)​w2,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}(\partial_{t}v,w_{2})_{(H^{-1}(\Omega),H_{0}^{1}(\Omega))}+\int_{Q_{T}}\nabla v.\nabla w_{2}=\int_{Q_{T}}f_{2}(u,v)w_{2},

Let (u,v)∈(WT∩L∞​(QT))2(u,v)\in(W_{T}\cap L^{\infty}(Q_{T}))^{2} and (u~,v~)∈(WT∩L∞​(QT))2(\widetilde{u},\widetilde{v})\in(W_{T}\cap L^{\infty}(Q_{T}))^{2} be two solutions of (NL). Then, (u,v)=(u~,v~)(u,v)=(\widetilde{u},\widetilde{v}).

Proof.

The nonlinearities f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} are in C∞​(ℝ2,ℝ)C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2},\mathbb{R}), thus they are locally Lipschitz on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. This provides the uniqueness of the solution of (NL) in L∞​(QT)L^{\infty}(Q_{T}) (associated to an initial data (u0,v0)∈L∞​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2} and a control h∈L2​(QT)h\in L^{2}(Q_{T})) by a Gronwall argument (see Section A.1). ∎

2.2. Main results

Our first main result is the following one.

Theorem 2.5.

The system (Odd) is globally null-controllable (in the sense of Definition 1.4).
More precisely, there exists (Cp)p∈[2,+∞)∈(0,∞)[2,+∞)(C_{p})_{p\in[2,+\infty)}\in(0,\infty)^{[2,+\infty)} such that for every initial data (u0,v0)∈L∞​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2}, there exists a control h∈⋂p∈[2,+∞)Lp(QT)h\in\bigcap\limits_{p\in[2,+\infty)}L^{p}(Q_{T}) satisfying

(11) ∀p∈[2,+∞),‖h‖Lp​(QT)≤Cp(‖u0‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)1/(2​k+1)),\forall p\in[2,+\infty),\ \left\lVert h\right\rVert_{L^{p}(Q_{T})}\leq C_{p}\left(\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\left\lVert v_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{1/(2k+1)}\right),

and the solution (u,v)(u,v) of (Odd) verifies

(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).
Remark 2.6.

We give some natural extensions of this result in Section 6.

Remark 2.7.

If we assume that

(12) Ω∈C2,α,\Omega\in C^{2,\alpha},

with 0<α<10<\alpha<1, then Theorem 2.5 remains true with a control h∈L∞​(QT)h\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T}) and the estimate (11) holds true with p=+∞p=+\infty (see Remark 3.9 and Remark 4.11).

Our second main result is a local controllability result for more general reaction-diffusion systems than (Odd).

Theorem 2.8.

Let (g1,g2)∈C∞​(ℝ,ℝ)2(g_{1},g_{2})\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{R})^{2} be such that

g1​(0)=g1′​(0)=⋯=g1(2​k)​(0)=0​and​g1(2​k+1)​(0)≠0,\displaystyle g_{1}(0)=g^{\prime}_{1}(0)=\dots=g_{1}^{(2k)}(0)=0\ \text{and}\ g_{1}^{(2k+1)}(0)\neq 0,
g2​(0)≠0.\displaystyle g_{2}(0)\neq 0.

Let f1∈C∞​(ℝ2,ℝ)f_{1}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}), f2∈C∞​(ℝ2,ℝ)f_{2}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}) be such that

(13) ∀v∈ℝ,f1​(0,v)=0,\displaystyle\forall v\in\mathbb{R},\ f_{1}(0,v)=0,
(14) ∀(u,v)∈ℝ2,f2​(u,v):=g1​(u)​g2​(v).\displaystyle\forall(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\ f_{2}(u,v):=g_{1}(u)g_{2}(v).

Then, the system (NL) is locally null-controllable (in the sense of Definition 1.4).

By taking f1​(u,v)=−u2​k+1=−f2​(u,v)f_{1}(u,v)=-u^{2k+1}=-f_{2}(u,v), Theorem 2.8 shows the local null-controllability of a model for the non reversible chemical reaction (according to the law of mass action and the Fick’s law)

where uu and vv denote respectively the concentrations of the component UU and VV.
However, we can’t deduce from Theorem 2.8 a local null-controllability result (which is true for k=1k=1 thanks to [11, Theorem 1]) of a model for the reversible chemical reaction

which corresponds to f1​(u,v)=−u2​k+1+v=−f2​(u,v)f_{1}(u,v)=-u^{2k+1}+v=-f_{2}(u,v).
By taking f1​(u,v)=(k2−(2​k1+1))​u2​k1+1+(k5−(2​k1+1))​u2​k1+1​vk4f_{1}(u,v)=(k_{2}-(2k_{1}+1))u^{2k_{1}+1}+(k_{5}-(2k_{1}+1))u^{2k_{1}+1}v^{k_{4}} and f2​(u,v)=k3​u2​k1+1+(k6−k4)​u2​k1+1​vk4f_{2}(u,v)=k_{3}u^{2k_{1}+1}+(k_{6}-k_{4})u^{2k_{1}+1}v^{k_{4}} with k1k_{1}, k2k_{2}, k3k_{3}, k4k_{4}, k5k_{5}, k6k_{6} positive integers, Theorem 2.8 shows the local null-controllability of a model for the chemical reaction

{(2​k1+1)​U⇀k2​U+k3​V,(2​k1+1)​U+k4​V⇀k5​U+k6​V.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}(2k_{1}+1)U&\rightharpoonup k_{2}U+k_{3}V,\\ (2k_{1}+1)U+k_{4}V&\rightharpoonup k_{5}U+k_{6}V.\end{array}\right.

Remark 3.3.

There exists at least three proofs of Proposition 3.2. First, the common argument is the null-controllability of the heat equation in L2L^{2} proved independently by Gilles Lebeau, Luc Robbiano in 1995 (see [25] and [24]) and Andrei Fursikov, Oleg Imanuvilov in 1996 (see [20]). Then, the goal is to get a control in L∞L^{\infty}. The first method has been employed for the first time by Enrique Fernandez-Cara and Enrique Zuazua (see [19, Theorem 3.1]) and it is based on the local regularizing effect of the heat equation which leads to a refined observability inequality (see [19, Proposition 3.2]). The second method has been employed for the first time by Viorel Barbu (see [4]) and it is based on a Penalized Hilbert Uniqueness Method (see also [11, Section 3.1.2]). The more recent method is due to Olivier Bodart, Manuel Gonzalez-Burgos, Rosario Pérez-Garcia (see [6]) and it is sometimes called the fictitious control method (see [17, Section 2] for the Neumann case and [15]).

4. A control for the heat equation which is an odd power

The goal of this section is to prove Proposition 3.7. We assume in the following that τ=T\tau=T. First, we prove a new Carleman estimate in L2​k+2L^{2k+2} for the heat equation. This type of inequality comes from the usual Carleman inequality in L2L^{2} and parabolic regularity. Then, we get the existence of a control for the heat equation such that h12​k+1h^{\frac{1}{2k+1}} is regular by considering a penalized problem in L2​k+22​k+1L^{\frac{2k+2}{2k+1}}, which is a generalization of the usual Penalized Hilbert Uniqueness Method.

6. Some generalizations of the global null-controllability for “odd power systems”

In this section, we generalize Theorem 2.5 to other parabolic systems. We omit the proofs because in each case, it is a slight adaptation of the strategy of Section 3.

6.1. Linear parabolic operators

We present a natural generalization of the global null-controllability of (Odd) to more general linear parabolic operators than ∂t−Δ\partial_{t}-\Delta.

Proposition 6.1.

Let k∈ℕ∗k\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, (d1,d2)∈(0,+∞)2(d_{1},d_{2})\in(0,+\infty)^{2}, (b1,b2)∈(L∞​(QT)N)2(b_{1},b_{2})\in(L^{\infty}(Q_{T})^{N})^{2}, (a1,a2)∈L∞​(QT)2(a_{1},a_{2})\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})^{2}. Then,

{∂tu−d1​Δ​u+b1.∇u+a1​u=h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−d2​Δ​v+b2.∇v+a2​v=u2​k+1in⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-d_{1}\Delta u+b_{1}.\nabla u+a_{1}u=h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-d_{2}\Delta v+b_{2}.\nabla v+a_{2}v=u^{2k+1}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega,\end{array}\right.

is globally null-controllable.

The proof is based on a Carleman estimate different from the one in Proposition 4.3 which can be found in [18, Lemma 2.1].

6.2. Global null-controllability result for particular superlinearities

We state a global null-controllability result linked with the global null-controllability of the semilinear heat equation.

Proposition 6.2.

Let k∈ℕ∗k\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, f∈C∞​(ℝ,ℝ)f\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{R}) such that

f⁡(0)=0​and​f⁡(s)s​log3/2​(1+|s|)→0​when​|s|→+∞.f(0)=0\ \text{and}\ \frac{f(s)}{s\log^{3/2}(1+|s|)}\rightarrow 0\ \text{when}\ |s|\rightarrow+\infty.

Then,

{∂tu−Δ​u=f⁡(u)+h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−Δ​v=u2​k+1in⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=f(u)+h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta v=u^{2k+1}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega,\end{array}\right.

is globally null-controllable.

The proof is based on the global null-controllability of the semilinear heat equation with superlinearity as the function ff. Particularly, we can see [19, Theorem 1.2] proved by Enrique Fernandez-Cara and Enrique Zuazua or [18, Theorem 1.7].

6.3. Global null-controllability for all “power systems”

Let n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. We have seen that (Power), with nn an even integer, is not (globally) null-controllable by the maximum principle (see Proposition 1.9) but (Power), with nn an odd integer, is globally null-controllable (see Theorem 2.5). In this section, we consider the following system:

(PowerO) {∂tu−Δ​u=h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−Δ​v=|u|n−1​uin⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta v=|u|^{n-1}u&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega.\end{array}\right.
Definition 6.3.

The mapping Φn:x∈ℝ↦|x|n−1​x∈ℝ\Phi_{n}:x\in\mathbb{R}\mapsto|x|^{n-1}x\in\mathbb{R} is one-to-one. We note its inverse function Φn−1\Phi_{n}^{-1}.

Remark 6.4.

For nn an even integer, Φn​(u)=un\Phi_{n}(u)=u^{n} if u≥0u\geq 0 and Φn​(u)=−un\Phi_{n}(u)=-u^{n} if u<0u<0. Whereas for nn an odd power, Φn​(u)=un\Phi_{n}(u)=u^{n} for every u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}.

We have a generalization of Theorem 2.5.

Theorem 6.5.

The system (PowerO) is globally null-controllable (in the sense of Definition 1.4).
More precisely, there exists (Cp)p∈[2,+∞)∈(0,∞)[2,+∞)(C_{p})_{p\in[2,+\infty)}\in(0,\infty)^{[2,+\infty)} such that for every initial data (u0,v0)∈L∞​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2}, there exists a control h∈⋂p∈[2,+∞)Lp(QT)h\in\bigcap\limits_{p\in[2,+\infty)}L^{p}(Q_{T}) satisfying

(151) ∀p∈[2,+∞),‖h‖Lp​(QT)≤Cp(‖u0‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)1/n),\forall p\in[2,+\infty),\ \left\lVert h\right\rVert_{L^{p}(Q_{T})}\leq C_{p}\left(\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\left\lVert v_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{1/n}\right),

and the solution (u,v)(u,v) of (PowerO) verifies

(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).

The strategy of proof of Theorem 6.5 is the same as for Theorem 2.5. It is based on the following key result.

Proposition 6.6.

For every τ>0\tau>0, there exists Cτ>0C_{\tau}>0 such that
for every y0∈L∞​(Ω)y_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega), there exists a control hτ∈L∞​(Qτ)h_{\tau}\in L^{\infty}(Q_{\tau}) which verifies

‖Φn−1​(hτ)‖L∞​(Qτ)≤Cτ​‖y0‖L∞​(Ω)1/n,\displaystyle\left\lVert\Phi_{n}^{-1}(h_{\tau})\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(Q_{\tau})}\leq C_{\tau}\left\lVert y_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{1/n},
Φn−1(hτ)∈⋂p∈[2,+∞)Xτ,p,\displaystyle\Phi_{n}^{-1}(h_{\tau})\in\bigcap\limits_{p\in[2,+\infty)}X_{\tau,p},
∀p∈[2,+∞),∃Cτ,p>0,‖Φn−1(hτ)‖Xτ,p≤Cτ,p‖y0‖L∞​(Ω)1/n,\displaystyle\forall p\in[2,+\infty),\ \exists C_{\tau,p}>0,\ \left\lVert\Phi_{n}^{-1}(h_{\tau})\right\rVert_{X_{\tau,p}}\leq C_{\tau,p}\left\lVert y_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{1/n},
hτ(0,.)=hτ(τ,.)=0,\displaystyle h_{\tau}(0,.)=h_{\tau}(\tau,.)=0,
∀t∈[0,τ],supp(hτ(t,.))⊂⊂ω,\displaystyle\forall t\in[0,\tau],\ supp(h_{\tau}(t,.))\subset\subset\omega,

such that the solution y∈L∞​(Qτ)y\in L^{\infty}(Q_{\tau}) of (18) satisfies y(τ,.)=0y(\tau,.)=0.

The proof of Proposition 6.6 is a slight adaptation of Section 4. First, we get a Carleman estimate in Ln+1L^{n+1} (see Theorem 4.4). Secondly, we use a penalized duality method in L(n+1)/nL^{(n+1)/n} as in Section 4.2 taking into account that the antiderivative of the continuous mapping Φn−1\Phi_{n}^{-1} (see Definition 6.3) is the strictly convex function

x∈ℝ↦nn+1​|x|n+1n:={nn+1​exp⁡(n+1n​log⁡(|x|))if​x≠0,0if​x=0.x\in\mathbb{R}\mapsto\frac{n}{n+1}\left\lvert x\right\rvert^{\frac{n+1}{n}}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{c l}\frac{n}{n+1}\exp(\frac{n+1}{n}\log(\left\lvert x\right\rvert))&\mathrm{if}\ x\neq 0,\\ 0&\mathrm{if}\ x=0.\end{array}\right.

6.4. Global null-controllability for “even power systems” in ℂ\mathbb{C}

Let k∈ℕ∗k\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. We have seen in Proposition 1.9 that global null-controllability does not hold for

(Even) {∂tu−Δ​u=h​1ωin⁡(0,T)×Ω,∂tv−Δ​v=u2​kin⁡(0,T)×Ω,u,v=0on⁡(0,T)×∂Ω,(u,v)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u-\Delta u=h1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta v=u^{2k}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u,v=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u,v)(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega.\end{array}\right.

A natural question, asked by Luc Robbiano, is: what happens if we consider complex-valued functions? A positive answer i.e. a global null-controllability result for (Even) with k=1k=1 is given in [11] (see [11, Theorem 3]). Here, we want to generalize this result for every k∈ℕ∗k\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. We have the following result.

Theorem 6.7.

The system (Even) is globally null-controllable (in the sense of Definition 1.4).
More precisely, there exists (Cp)p∈[2,+∞)∈(0,∞)[2,+∞)(C_{p})_{p\in[2,+\infty)}\in(0,\infty)^{[2,+\infty)} such that for every initial data (u0,v0)∈L∞​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2}, there exists a control h∈⋂p∈[2,+∞)Lp(QT;ℂ)h\in\bigcap\limits_{p\in[2,+\infty)}L^{p}(Q_{T};\mathbb{C}) satisfying

(152) ∀p∈[2,+∞),‖h‖Lp​(QT,ℂ)≤Cp(‖u0‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)1/(2​k)),\forall p\in[2,+\infty),\ \left\lVert h\right\rVert_{L^{p}(Q_{T};\mathbb{C})}\leq C_{p}\left(\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\left\lVert v_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{1/(2k)}\right),

and the solution (u,v)∈L∞​(QT,ℂ)2(u,v)\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T},\mathbb{C})^{2} of (Even) verifies

(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).(u,v)(T,.)=(0,0).

The strategy of proof of Theorem 6.7 is the same as for Theorem 2.5 (see Section 3). The first step of the proof i.e. Section 3.1 does not change but we have to modify some arguments given in Section 3.2.
Let us fix (u0,v0)∈L∞​(Ω)2(u_{0},v_{0})\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)^{2} until the end of the section.

6.4.1. First step of the proof: steer uu to 00

First, we find a control of (Even) which steers uu to 00 in time T/2T/2 (see the proof of Proposition 3.1).

There exists h1∈L∞​((0,T/2)×Ω,ℝ)h_{1}\in L^{\infty}((0,T/2)\times\Omega;\mathbb{R}) satisfying

such that the solution (u1,v1)∈L∞​((0,T/2)×Ω,ℝ)2(u_{1},v_{1})\in L^{\infty}((0,T/2)\times\Omega;\mathbb{R})^{2} of

{∂tu1−Δ​u1=h1​1ωin⁡(0,T/2)×Ω,∂tv1−Δ​v1=u12​kin⁡(0,T/2)×Ω,u1,v1=0on⁡(0,T/2)×∂Ω,(u1,v1)(0,.)=(u0,v0)in​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u_{1}-\Delta u_{1}=h_{1}1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T/2)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v_{1}-\Delta v_{1}=u_{1}^{2k}&\mathrm{in}\ (0,T/2)\times\Omega,\\ u_{1},v_{1}=0&\mathrm{on}\ (0,T/2)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u_{1},v_{1})(0,.)=(u_{0},v_{0})&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega,\end{array}\right.

satisfies u1(T/2,.)=0u_{1}(T/2,.)=0. Moreover, we have

The aim of this part is to find a complex control of (Even) which steers vv to 00 (and uu from 00 to 00) in time TT.

Proposition 6.9.

Let ((u1,v1),h1)((u_{1},v_{1}),h_{1}) as in Proposition 6.8.
There exists a control h2∈⋂p∈[2,+∞)Lp((T/2,T)×Ω;ℂ)h_{2}\in\bigcap_{p\in[2,+\infty)}L^{p}((T/2,T)\times\Omega;\mathbb{C}) satisfying

(155) ∀p∈[2,+∞),‖h2‖OPENLp​((T/2,T)×Ω);ℂ)≤Cp(‖u0‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)1/(2​k)).\forall p\in[2,+\infty),\ \left\lVert h_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{p}((T/2,T)\times\Omega);\mathbb{C})}\leq C_{p}\left(\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\left\lVert v_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{1/(2k)}\right).

such that the solution (u2,v2)∈L∞​((T/2,T)×Ω,ℂ)2(u_{2},v_{2})\in L^{\infty}((T/2,T)\times\Omega;\mathbb{C})^{2} of

{∂tu2−Δ​u2=h2​1ωin⁡(T/2,T)×Ω,∂tv2−Δ​v2=u22​kin⁡(T/2,T)×Ω,u2,v2=0on⁡(T/2,T)×∂Ω,(u2,v2)(T/2,.)=(0,v1(T/2,.))in​Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l}\partial_{t}u_{2}-\Delta u_{2}=h_{2}1_{\omega}&\mathrm{in}\ (T/2,T)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v_{2}-\Delta v_{2}=u_{2}^{2k}&\mathrm{in}\ (T/2,T)\times\Omega,\\ u_{2},v_{2}=0&\mathrm{on}\ (T/2,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ (u_{2},v_{2})(T/2,.)=(0,v_{1}(T/2,.))&\mathrm{in}\ \Omega,\end{array}\right.

satisfies (u2,v2)(T,.)=(0,0)(u_{2},v_{2})(T,.)=(0,0).

Our approach consists in looking at the second equation of (Odd) like a controlled heat equation where the state is v(t,.)v(t,.) and the control input is u2​k(t,.)u^{2k}(t,.). Here, the question consists in proving that the heat equation is null-controllable with a localized control which is as an even power of a regular complex function.

Now, we can prove Proposition 6.9.
